newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Grain - Prices flat, Indonesian corn up.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Prices flat, Indonesian corn up.

text.p: Domestic grains and oilseeds prices were steady to easier in Malaysia and Thailand this week, but Indonesian corn prices were higher on tight supply, traders said on Wednesday.
"When prices are going down, normally no one wants to buy and I haven't heard of anything this week," said a dealer with a Kuala Lumpur flour mill.
Another trader said players were likely to be more confident of committing to further purchases after the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) releases its next crop report on November 12.
"The market is likely to be quiet until then," he said.
"A" grade wheat in bags was holding firm at 840 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown central region. Low-grade wheat was quoted at 500-510 ringgit a tonne.
Local soymeal was indicated at 818 ringgit a tonne while imported soymeal was going for about 810 ringgit.
Bulk corn was trading at 500-505 ringgit.
Thai soymeal prices were steady to lower as more animal feed ingredients arrived, while increased local supply pushed local corn prices down, trade sources in Bangkok said.

Corn prices dipped to 4.35-4.38 baht a kg from 4.40-4.45 baht a kg last week. Traders said prices eased as more corn entered the market after floods began to subside. Floods have ravaged many parts of Thailand since the monsoon season started in late May.
Soymeal prices were quoted around 10.20 baht a kg from 10.20-10.30 baht a week earlier.

The industry seems reluctant to place new orders at the moment, dealers said. Despite some tightness in Thai soybean supplies, many said they were comfortable as more feed ingredients have arrived or will come in soon.
"We are well-covered for the year. But we might buy more if we receive any sign or assurances that the new tariff scheme will be effective by November 1 as scheduled," one feed producer said.

The Thai cabinet earlier this month eliminated import quotas on raw feed material and cut import tariffs on soybean, soymeal and corn effective on November 1. Government sources said on Tuesday the new tariff scheme will be implemented on schedule.
At least 90,000 tonnes of imported feed ingredients such as soymeal, wheat and corn gluten meal had arrived in Thailand since the beginning of October.
An additional 7,867 tonnes of groundnut meal, sunflower meal and soymeal from India is scheduled to arrive on Thursday.
Next month, nearly 145,000 tonnes of soymeal and soy pellets are expected to arrive at Thai ports.

The vessel Northern Light is scheduled to arrive with 25,193 tonnes of Argentine low-protein soymeal on November 8. Kavo Kaliakra is also on the way from Brazil with 53,789 tonnes of soy pellets and is expected to arrive on November 11.
The ship Vega T will arrive around November 23 with 20,000 tonnes of Brazil-origin soymeal and Toscana is expected to arrive on November 25 with an identical cargo from Argentina.
One trader said he expected more buying orders to emerge if soymeal prices, especially for Indian-origin, fell further.
"Prices have eased so far but many believe they could go lower,' he said, adding that U.S. soymeal is being quoted at $310 a tonne C&F Bangkok while Indian soymeal is quoted around $290 a tonne C&F.
In Indonesia, corn prices moved higher in Jakarta on tight supply coupled with rising demand at the end of harvests in the key growing regions in Java and Sumatra, traders said.
They said corn was quoted at 430-435 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, up from 420-425 rupiah from a week ago. Soymeal, however, was sharply lower at 820 rupiah/kg from 850 rupiah on ample supply.
"The corn market has been rather active with about 500 tonnes traded daily," one trader said. "The end of the harvest in East Java and Lampung (in Sumatra) has squeezed supplies."

He said imported corn supply was limited due to washouts by local buyers, but added that one player who could not cancel his contract was expected to take delivery of 30,000 to 40,000 tonnes in December.
Traders said the next harvests in both the growing regions in Java and Sumatra were expected in February-March.
One trader said Indian origin soymeal was on offer at $300-$302/tonne C&F Jakarta.
